newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Air Force expands flight suspension area.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Air Force expands flight suspension area.

text.p: The Air Force on Monday expanded a suspension of flight training off the East Coast to include the Gulf of Mexico after additional reports of air incidents involving civilian planes and military jets.

The Air Force confirmed a CNN report of two more incidents on Friday in which an F-16 fighter jet got closer than five miles (8.047 km) to a Northwest Airlines Airbus over Texas and two other F-16s came within 3.5 miles (5.633 km) of an American Airlines plane over New Mexico.

Two other incidents on Wednesday and Friday off the East Coast involving commercial aircraft and F-16 Air National Guard jets prompted the Air Force on Friday to halt operations in all designed training areas off that coast.

The Air Force, which insists that no "near-collisions" have occurred, said in a brief announcement on Monday that operations were now suspended in training areas of both the Gulf and East Coasts pending a review of procedures with the Federal Aviation Administration and military controllers.
"There is now a very heightened awareness out there and sightings are being reported by commercial pilots," said one Pentagon official, who asked not to be identified.

The FAA on Friday ordered controllers at its Jacksonville, Florida, Washington and New York air traffic control centers and military controllers at the Virginia Capes station to review procedures for handling traffic.

That FAA order came hours after an American Eagle pilot reported that four national guard F-16 jets flew "too close" to his passenger plane off the coast of Delaware in the second such incident in three days.

Last Wednesday, the operator of a Boeing 727 charter jet with about 80 passengers on board said it came very close to two F-16s off the coast of New Jersey. It maneuvered violently in response to electronic cockpit instrument warnings when it was approached by one of the national guard fighters.

The FAA said on Friday the American Eagle commercial plane, flying from Raleigh, North Carolina, to John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, reported that the military jets came too close as he flew at an altitude of about 19,000 feet (5,791 metres).

At the Pentagon, however, the commander of the U.S. Air National Guard said "there was no imminent collision" and that the four fighters from the District of Columbia Air National Guard did not come dangerously close to the twin-engine plane.
"My opinion about flight off the East Coast is that it is very safe," Air Force Maj. Gen. Donald Shepperd said in response to questions from reporters, before the flight suspension was announced.

Shepperd said at the Pentagon that the four F-16s returned normally to their base at Andrews Air Force Base, Maryland, after Friday's incident, which occurred at about 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT) about 15 miles (24 km) east of the Maryland coast over the Atlantic Ocean.
Shepperd said both incidents were under investigation and he had no indication any of the military pilots had done anything wrong. Civilian aviation authorities were also investigating the reports.
"All four of the F-16s had the airliner in sight, I would like to stress that," he said. "And they proceeded and landed normally at home."

He said the American Eagle commercial plane was at an altitude of about 19,000 feet (5,791 metres) and three of the jets flew over it, but were at least 2,000 feet (610 metres) above the commercial plane.
The fourth F-16, he said, was ahead of the American Eagle flight at an altitude of about 17,500 feet (5,334 metres) and was descending.
